idea: A river meander simulated in code until it loops back on itself and leaves oxbow lakes behind, one clean line, with the caption 'Einstein explained why rivers bend. With a teacup. 1926.' (his paper on meanders and Baer's law). For people who like a famous mind caught on a small domestic problem.

One year of tide height at a single port drawn as one unbroken wave, built from a sum of sine constituents, the fat spring tides swelling into thin neaps. Caption: 'Kelvin built a machine to add these up. 1872.' (his tide-predicting machine of brass pulleys and cord).

A loxodrome: a ship holding one constant compass bearing, drawn on a globe as a spiral that winds toward the pole without ever reaching it. Caption: 'Constant bearing. Never arrives. Pedro Nunes, 1537.' A sailor's joke about commitment that is also true geometry.

A ship's wake rendered as a simulated wave field with its V of two lines, and the angle marked: '19.47°'. Smaller text: 'Every ship. Any speed.' (the Kelvin wake half-angle in deep water). A fact that sounds invented and is not.

A Fresnel lighthouse lens as concentric prismatic rings generated in code, in the manner of an engineer's section. Caption: 'Cordouan, 1823. First Fresnel lens.' For lighthouse people who want the optics, not the postcard.

Thirteen stacked sea traces generated procedurally, labelled 0 to 12, from a flat line to chaos, with the original Beaufort wording for force 0: 'Sea like a mirror.' Header: 'Beaufort, 1805.' A scale you can wear and point at on a bad day.

A chambered nautilus shell cross-section drawn by code as a true logarithmic spiral with each chamber wall, captioned 'Not the golden ratio. Go measure it.' A point-of-view shirt aimed at everyone who has seen that myth printed on a mug.

Every position from European ship logbooks 1750-1850 (the CLIWOC dataset) plotted as points on a blank page, so the oceans fill with traffic and the coastlines appear as empty space. Caption: 'No map. Only logbooks.' A map made of absences.

A grid of weather cells over Europe as a hand-ruled numerical forecast table, captioned 'Richardson, 1922: predicted a 145 hPa change in six hours. The barometer did not move.' (his first numerical weather forecast, done by hand and wrong). Honest about how forecasting began.

The coast of Britain drawn four times with shrinking rulers, each outline longer than the last. Caption: 'How long is the coast of Britain? Depends on your ruler.' (Mandelbrot's 1967 paper, after Richardson). For people who like a question with no clean answer.

A sailing-ship hull as a lines plan (body plan, half-breadth and sheer), generated by code from a parametric hull with every station curve. Caption: 'Every curve is a promise about water.' Nods to Chapman's Architectura Navalis Mercatoria, 1768.

Flow lines of the Gulf Stream traced by particle simulation as a river inside the ocean, captioned 'Ask the whalers. Franklin's Gulf Stream chart, 1770.' (drawn from Nantucket captain Timothy Folger's knowledge). For people who like it when the working crew knew first.

Co-tidal lines of the North Sea radiating like a clock face around a point in the middle, computed from a simple rotating-wave model. Caption: 'Tides turn around a point where there is no tide.' (amphidromic points, mapped by Whewell in 1833).

Waves entering a harbour mouth simulated as a ripple-tank line drawing, the swell fanning into calm water behind the breakwater. Caption: 'Harbour: a gap the width of one wave.' For anyone who has stood on a mole and wondered why it is quiet inside.

Stacked bathymetric profile lines across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, ridge-and-rift in ridge-line relief, from public ocean-depth data. Caption: 'Marie Tharp drew the rift valley in 1952-57. Heezen called it girl talk.' A shirt with a point of view about who gets believed.

A school of simulated herring turning as one around a lone predator, each fish following three local rules and no leader. Caption: 'No one is in charge. Craig Reynolds, 1986.' (the boids model). For people who like order that nobody ordered.

Meridians of longitude drawn as a clock face, captioned 'Four seconds of time is one nautical mile.' (at the equator, since the Earth turns 15 degrees an hour). The whole longitude problem in one line, for people who like to know why Harrison mattered.

Every Atlantic hurricane track since 1851 (HURDAT2) overlaid as thin lines on a blank page, the basin and its coastlines emerging from the storms alone. Caption: 'Every Atlantic hurricane since 1851. No coastline drawn.'

The Draupner rogue wave as a plain trace of the sea surface, a calm record and then one spike, with the label '1 January 1995, 25.6 m'. Smaller text: 'Sailors said so for centuries.' (first measured wave of its kind, by laser on a North Sea platform).

A yacht polar diagram drawn as a clean boat-speed curve around a compass, with a blank wedge dead ahead into the wind labelled 'No-go zone'. Caption: 'No boat sails straight into the wind. The good ones sail around it.' For sailors, and for anyone with a point to make about detours.
